exam: A 22‑year‑old primigravida in a rural clinic has not saved transport money. What should you do next? — Arrange community transport voucher, document in her antenatal card, and schedule a follow‑up to confirm readiness.

During labour a woman reports sudden heavy bleeding and cannot reach the planned hospital. What are the immediate actions? — Activate emergency referral, give uterotonics if PPH suspected, start IV fluids, and inform receiving facility of likely hemorrhage.

You discover a woman is HIV positive at 28 weeks. How does this affect her birth‑preparedness plan? — Ensure antiretroviral prophylaxis, plan delivery at a facility with infection‑control measures, and arrange newborn prophylaxis.

A woman in labour presents with a blood pressure of 150/100 mmHg but no proteinuria. What does this mean for her BPCR? — Consider pre‑eclampsia risk; arrange delivery at a centre capable of caesarean section and monitor closely.
Explain how you would counsel a family that prefers home birth but lacks a clean delivery kit. — Provide a kit, teach its use, and discuss the need for rapid transfer if complications arise.

A community health worker reports that most women do not know the signs of neonatal sepsis. What intervention aligns with BPCR? — Conduct group education on neonatal danger signs and distribute printed leaflets.
During a post‑natal visit you find the mother has not saved any cash for emergencies. What is your recommendation? — Link her to a community savings group or micro‑loan scheme and document the plan.

A woman in labour arrives at the facility after a 6‑hour delay due to transport failure. What key points do you document for audit? — Time of decision to seek care, transport mode, delays encountered, and outcome; use this to improve community transport plans.
ai.title: Birth Preparedness and Complication Readiness
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Birth preparedness equips pregnant women and families to plan safe delivery and respond to emergencies. It reduces delays, improves maternal‑newborn outcomes, and is essential in low‑resource settings.

b: Goal: reduce first‑delay (decision‑making) and second‑delay (reaching care).
Core components: birth location, skilled attendant, transport, funds, emergency supplies, and danger‑sign awareness.
sections.p: Birth preparedness and complication readiness (BPCR) is a community‑based strategy that encourages women, families and health workers to identify a birth plan, recognize danger signs, and arrange transport, finances and a skilled birth attendant.

b: Identify preferred delivery site and confirm it has emergency obstetric care (EmOC).
Arrange transport (e.g., boda‑boda, ambulance) before labour starts.
Save cash or identify a community fund for fees, drugs and supplies.
Prepare clean delivery kit (blade, cord clamp, sterile gloves, clean surface).
Teach at least three danger signs for mother and newborn.
sections.p: BPCR integrates antenatal counseling, community mobilisation, and health‑system linkages. In low‑resource hospitals, clinicians must verify that each component is in place and reinforce it at every visit.

b: Missing transport plan → second‑delay, higher maternal mortality.
No skilled attendant → increased risk of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) mismanagement.
Unrecognized danger signs → delayed referral for obstructed labour, eclampsia, sepsis.
sections.p: During antenatal visits, clinicians assess BPCR status, correct gaps, and document plans. In labour, the birth plan guides rapid referral if complications arise.

b: Explain three maternal danger signs and three neonatal danger signs.
Describe how to document a BPCR checklist in the antenatal card.
Outline immediate steps when a woman in labour cannot reach the planned facility.
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to apply BPCR to a vignette, to counsel patients, and to manage a complication when the plan fails.

b: Assuming all facilities have blood transfusion – verify availability.
Neglecting cultural preferences that may affect transport or facility choice.
Over‑relying on community health workers without confirming their training.
sections.p: Students often list BPCR items without linking them to clinical decision‑making or forget to adapt the plan to local resources.
BPCR itself does not require laboratory tests, but clinicians must use routine antenatal investigations to inform the plan.

t.b: Is the mother anemic? → anemia >11 g/dL requires iron, may affect PPH risk.
Is there pre‑eclampsia? → +1 protein + hypertension → arrange delivery at a facility with caesarean capability.
Is the mother HIV positive? → plan for antiretroviral prophylaxis and safe delivery practices.
Gestational age and fetal position → decide on facility with emergency obstetric care.

b: Counsel on danger signs; give written checklist.
Arrange transport voucher or community driver contract.
Secure funds: encourage saving or link to micro‑finance.
Provide clean delivery kit and teach its use.
If labour occurs away from the planned site, activate emergency referral and inform receiving facility of expected complications.
sections.p: BPCR is preventive; management focuses on reinforcing the plan and acting promptly when complications occur.

b: Antenatal care: clinical monitoring and screening.
Birth preparedness: logistical planning and emergency readiness.
sections.p: Birth preparedness is not the same as routine antenatal care, though they overlap.

b: Normal blood pressure does not rule out rapid‑onset pre‑eclampsia.
No reported bleeding does not exclude concealed haemorrhage.
sections.p: Absence of reported danger signs does not guarantee safety; silent complications (e.g., silent uterine rupture) can occur.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache or visual disturbance
